THOUGHT: This 17-year-old male presents with progressive upper extremity weakness and sensory loss for several months following a motor vehicle accident 4 months ago. Notably, initial evaluation was unrevealing, but symptoms have since evolved — a red flag for a delayed-onset neurological process. The pattern is highly selective: profound motor and sensory deficits confined to the upper extremities (strength 1/5, decreased sensation), with preserved lower extremity strength and sensation, intact cranial nerves, and normal reflexes. This dissociated sensory-motor pattern — affecting arms more than legs — strongly suggests a central cord lesion disrupting crossing fibers in the cervical spinal cord. The MRI cervical spine revealing a syrinx is the pivotal finding. A syrinx is a fluid-filled cavity within the spinal cord parenchyma; post-traumatic syringomyelia is a well-documented complication of spinal cord injury, often presenting months to years after trauma due to altered CSF dynamics and progressive cord expansion. The syrinx typically begins in the cervical region and expands centrifugally, preferentially damaging the crossing spinothalamic tract (causing bilateral upper extremity sensory loss) and anterior horn cells (causing lower motor neuron–type weakness in hands/arms), while sparing long tracts to the legs early on — matching this patient’s clinical picture. Other considerations (e.g., Guillain-Barré, ALS, cervical disc herniation, MS, tumor) are less likely: GBS usually involves ascending weakness and autonomic features (not seen here; also no elevated CSF protein or nerve conduction abnormalities reported); ALS would show upper + lower motor signs and progression to legs/bulbar regions; MS typically has multifocal, relapsing symptoms and characteristic white matter lesions on brain/spine MRI — not isolated syrinx; compressive myelopathy from disc or stenosis would more likely show hyperreflexia or long-tract signs (e.g., Babinski, spasticity), which are absent. His hypotension (90/60) and tachycardia (HR 115) may reflect autonomic dysregulation from chronic spinal cord pathology or deconditioning, but are nonspecific. Normal labs and imaging (except MRI) further support a structural intramedullary process rather than metabolic, inflammatory, or infectious etiology.

DIAGNOSIS: Post-traumatic syringomyelia
